correctness.rationale: The initial closed-neighborhood observation of a mixed set leaves at most one missing vertex on either bipartition, each then forced by an observed vertex having one unseen neighbor (n>=3). A one-sided t>=2 set observes the whole opposite side, with r=n-t remaining same-side vertices. If r>=k+2 every observed opposite vertex has >=k+1 unseen neighbors, so the process cannot advance; if r<=k+1 a matched-nonedge observed vertex forces all but one, then another forces the last. A singleton has n-2 unseen neighbors from each observed opposite vertex and succeeds exactly for k>=n-2. These cases are exhaustive and justify the polynomial and minima. Independently implemented set-closure enumeration checked all 145600 subsets/parameter instances for 3<=n<=7, distinct from the bundled n<=8 check; finite computation not infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The canonical 2019 crown-paper indexed theorem reports n-k as the minimum, contradicted by a mixed pair at n=5,k=1 under the explicitly stated standard generalized propagation convention. General 2012 introduction and 2013 regular-graph bound supply terminology and upper bounds, but not complete all-set profiles. Brimkov et al. develop ordinary power-domination polynomials without the generalized crown-family enumerator. Published Resultary crown results use restrained or Roman domination, while a chain-graph k-power-domination result concerns graphs with nested neighborhoods (not crowns for n>=3). Full 2019 publisher PDF remains inaccessible due to verification layer, so no whole-document absence is asserted.
residual_risks: Full 2019 primary PDF was blocked by interactive publisher verification, so its other potentially relevant results are not excluded by full-text inspection.
Any alternative k-power-domination convention would require rechecking the contradiction; review explicitly uses the standard <=k unobserved neighbors rule.
